Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 256 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 256 ‘Islay’ (WMU 256) covers an area of 2,700 km2 and is located in east-central 
Alberta, primarily in the Central Parkland natural subregion. The WMU is delineated by the North Saskatchewan 
River to the north, the Alberta-Saskatchewan interprovincial boundary to the east, Highway 16 to the south, and 
Highway 41 to the west. Agriculture is predominant throughout the unit covering 72% of the landscape, then 
grassland and developed areas covering 11% and 9 % respectively. Urban centres include Lloydminster and 
Vermilion, as well as several small communities. Oil and gas extraction activities occur primarily on private 
agricultural land. Sensitive wildlife areas include Great Blue Heron Colonial Nesting sites, and a Key Wildlife 
Biodiversity Zone (55 km²) is designated along the North Saskatchewan River.  
 
The objective of the 2018/19 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate (moose, white-tailed deer, mule deer) 
population in WMU 256 by estimating abundance, density and the age-sex composition. 
 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted December 17 to 19, 2018 using distance sampling techniques 
(Buckland et al., 2001, Thomas et al., 2010). A total of 149 north-south transect lines (survey effort = 1,261.7 
kilometres) were flown with two jet ranger helicopters, each outfitted with rear bubble windows to maximize 
visibility. Ungulates were classified by age class (adult or juvenile) and sex. Other wildlife sightings were recorded. 
 
Results 
Moose 
A total of 82 moose were observed in 39 groups and classified as 13 bulls (all with antlers), 33 cows, and 36 
calves. The estimated bull:cow:calf ratio was 39:100:109. The estimated density was 0.112 moose/km2 (90% CI 
0.077 – 0.164) and the estimated abundance was 303 moose (90% CI 207 – 443, Table 1).  
 
White-tailed deer 
A total of 529 white-tailed deer were observed in 169 groups and classified as 50 bucks (all with antlers), 292 
does, 169 fawns, and 18 unclassified adults. The estimated buck:doe:fawn ratio was 17:100:58. Although antler 
drop was assumed to be minimal, the buck ratio is likely underestimated. The estimated density was 0.824 white-
tailed deer/km2 (90% CI 0.662 – 1.025) and estimated abundance was 2,225 white-tailed deer (90% CI 1,788 – 
2,767).  
 
Mule deer 
A total of 461 mule deer were observed in 99 groups and classified as 56 bucks (all with antlers), 217 does, 151 
fawns, and 37 unclassified adults. The estimated buck:doe:fawn ratio was 26:100:70. Although antler drop was 
assumed to be minimal, the buck ratio is likely underestimated. The estimated density was 0.694 mule deer/km2 
(90% CI 0.534 – 0.901) and estimated abundance was 1,874 mule deer (90% CI 1,443 – 2,433).
